extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers and NIH grant applicants (graduate students, postdocs, new investigators)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical overview of how NIH study sections review grant applications and what applicants should know to target their writing and outreach. Emphasizes study section selection, reviewer roles/timelines, scoring/triage, special panels, and practical tactics (e.g., contacting program officers, networking with appointed members).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate study section (match focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you click on a specific study section you will first find a description of the areas of focus for that panel. This is the place to start your research into how your grant applications are likely to be reviewed and therefore how you should write them!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the CSR roster pages to identify the panels whose areas of focus match your application. Familiarize yourself with typical study sections to which you might submit and the types of reviewers on those panels; doing this should guide how you write your application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the appointed members and their interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The appointed members are scientists who have accepted an invitation to serve on each meeting of the panel for a four year period.... These individuals form the core of the study section culture and have the greatest overall impact on review behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn what these people work on and where their scientific interests lie. If you don't know them, try to meet them at meetings or introduce yourself; personal contact can help connect a face with your application. You might even ask them to have a coffee to discuss grant review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand dated rosters and the role of ad hoc reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The dated panels include the appointed members who were actually reviewing grants that round as well as an additional number of ad hoc reviewers generally indicated with an asterix... The ad hoc reviewers serve to enhance the breadth of the panel based upon the grants that have been assigned for that particular round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the dated roster appended to your summary statement to see who actually reviewed that round. Ad hoc reviewers may review by phone or only provide a single review; they may be new, frequent ad hocs, or former appointed members. Use patterns of ad hoc selection to 'suss out' likely reviewer types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment to three reviewers and review timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Your grant gets assigned to 3 reviewers who receive your grant about 6 weeks prior to the study section meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers read each proposal, prepare a narrative critique and a preliminary score. Preliminary scores and critiques are submitted about one week prior to the meeting in the electronic reviewer system (eRA Commons). All assigned reviewers can then read each other's critiques and may modify their positions before the meeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary scoring format (how reviewers score pre-meeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: They carefully and thoughtfully read each proposal, assigning both a narrative critique and a preliminary score to each application. Eventual scores range from 100 (excellent) to 500 (not so). Reviewers use single unit with one decimal point scores- 1.2, 2.4, etc which will eventually translate into the familiar 120, 240 scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the numeric scoring conventions and how preliminary scores are entered; preliminary scores influence triage and discussion decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage: many applications are not discussed
rubrics_metrics.description: A triage line is drawn. Currently about 60% of applications are not scheduled for discussion at the meeting and will (generally) not receive a score. The remaining 40% will be further discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Getting into the discussed group is critical; non-discussed (triaged) apps typically do not receive a score. Tailor your application to avoid easy triage by making significance/approach/innovation clear and compelling to reviewers reading remotely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion, post-discussion scoring, and full-panel vote
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants are discussed with each reviewer presenting his or her review... The three reviewers then issue their 'post-discussion' scores which, hopefully, describe a range with even better agreement than the initial scores. The entire panel votes within the range of post-discussion scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The in-meeting discussion can materially change scores; reviewers present, debate, and other panel members chime in. Aim to anticipate likely criticisms so reviewers' presentations and the ensuing discussion favorably frame your application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Emphasis Panels (SEPs) and RFAs review arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: RFA apps are reviewed in specially convened sections called Special Emphasis Panels. I am not familiar with any RFAs sending to established panels but it wouldn’t shock me if some did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are recurring SEPs (listed on CSR) and many RFAs are reviewed by internal Institute SEPs; rosters for these panels are often formed after the submission deadline so you may not be able to know in advance who will review. Check era.nih.gov roster pages for institute SEPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use CSR and eRA Commons resources to research sections and rosters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Center for Scientific Review of the NIH administers the workings of the majority of panels. A list is here: http://www.csr.nih.gov/Roster_proto/sectionI.asp ... Click on the 'roster' link and you will find additional links to the appointed member rosters as well as the rosters for three of the most-recent meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start your research at CSR pages to identify likely panels and review recent rosters to see who actually reviewed specific rounds. The dated roster is appended to summary statements you receive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your Program Officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t forget to talk to your Program Officer at whatever institute your grant is going to. They can often tell you what kinds of grants are going to get funded and what aren’t as well as pay-lines and all other sorts of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers are a source of inside information on funding likelihood and pay-lines; it is permissible to email them and exchange communications. Note they avoid making promises of funding until awards are issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the application readable and test comprehension with colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: You simply have no choice but to take responsibility for their failure to understand what you were trying to tell them... I suggest that you have your grant read by other people in your field–but not your subfield–to see how it reads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reviewers misunderstand your proposal, it's usually a writing problem. Have colleagues (especially those not in your narrow subfield) read the application to ensure clarity; revise to make arguments and solutions unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of study section membership dynamics and long-term strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervals of service overlap such that there are always individuals rotating off after the June/July meetings and other individuals rotating into service during the October/November meetings... Remember, you are in this for the long haul so think beyond a single study section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because review panels rotate and culture is driven by appointed members, develop a multi-year strategy: build relationships, consider which sections you target over time, and track who is likely to be on panels in future rounds.
